claims.text: The baseline is a refractory high-entropy alloy with a homogeneous, primarily single-phase microstructure and no titanium addition.
Approximately 1 at.% titanium is incorporated into the alloy during synthesis.
Adding approximately 1 at.% titanium will induce in situ formation of nanoscale Ti-rich precipitates.
The Ti-rich precipitates will be coherent with the surrounding microstructure.
The Ti-rich precipitates will be distributed within grains and along grain boundaries.
The titanium addition promotes nucleation of fine precipitates.
The fine precipitates impede dislocation motion at high temperature.
The fine precipitates suppress grain-boundary sliding at high temperature.
Impeded dislocation motion and suppressed grain-boundary sliding increase high-temperature creep strength.
The titanium-modified alloy will improve high-temperature mechanical strength or creep resistance by roughly 20–30% relative to the titanium-free baseline.
The expected high-temperature benefit will hold at approximately 800–1000°C under constant load relevant to jet-turbine applications.
Approximately 1 at.% titanium will leave room-temperature mechanical properties nearly unchanged.
Approximately 1 at.% titanium will leave alloy density nearly unchanged.
The beneficial effects occur only within a narrow titanium-addition range near 1 at.%.
Higher titanium contents may cause excessive precipitate formation or brittle intermetallic phases.
Excessive precipitates or brittle intermetallic phases at higher titanium contents may degrade room-temperature performance.
Precipitate formation and the resulting improvement may be sensitive to processing conditions, alloy composition, and thermal history.
